**Case:** Hopwood v. Texas, October Term 1996; Fifth Circuit No. 94-50664, 78 F.3d 932, reviewing the judgment at 861 F. Supp. 551. Merits decision, November 25, 1996. On review of the Fifth Circuit’s judgment of March 18, 1996; rehearing denied April 4, 1996. No argument date or separate Supreme Court docket number is established in this account.

**Questions:** Whether racial and ethnic educational diversity can be a compelling interest in public-university admissions; whether race-conscious preferences may remedy past discrimination and what predicate and necessity must be shown; and whether the law school’s 1992 system was constitutional and what relief the affected applicants may obtain. The related intervention appeal, No. 94-50569, is outside the grant.

**Record and posture:** Four white Texas applicants—Cheryl Hopwood, Douglas Carvell, Kenneth Elliott and David Rogers—challenge the 1992 process in an individual, nonclass suit. They sought declaration, injunction, admission, compensatory damages and punitive damages under the Equal Protection Clause, §§1981 and 1983 and Title VI. The named defendants include State entities and officials in their official capacities. The District Court found the separate discretionary-review machinery unlawful, awarded one dollar nominal damages to each applicant, declaratory relief and fee-free reapplication, and refused compensation, punitive damages, admission and a broad injunction. The Fifth Circuit remanded individual causation under a school-borne preponderance burden, rejected diversity and the offered remedial grounds, retained the punitive and injunction denials, and left Eleventh Amendment immunity undecided.

In March 1992, resident presumptive-admit index thresholds were 199 for white and other nonpreferred applicants and 189 for Black and Mexican-American applicants; presumptive-deny thresholds were 192 and 179. Earlier preferred-group thresholds varied. Score categories admitted exceptions: some presumptive-admit files moved to discretionary review, and some low-score files could move upward. The preferred groups had separate discretionary review and waiting lists. Enrollment aspirations and observed percentages were not proved fixed reserved seats. How different waiting lists were compared for final places is not fully established. Hopwood’s 199 index led to discretionary review after an assessment of her educational background; the other applicants had indexes of 197. The later program changed the old arrangements, but its full operation is not before the Court.

DeAngelis v. El Paso Municipal Police Officers' Association; Fifth Circuit No. 93-8700. Argued October 15, 1996; decided January 6, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Fifth Circuit, which reversed the jury's Title VII verdict and rendered judgment for the Association, 51 F.3d 591. The questions concern hostile-environment sufficiency, the preserved First Amendment defense to publication-based liability, and retaliation through references to DeAngelis's discrimination complaint.

The challenged newsletter reached at least seven hundred officers. The ten reproduced columns, including the April 1990 item, included derogatory comments about women generally and references connected to DeAngelis. She described humiliation, reduced confidence, promotion hesitation, mocking and impaired supervisory authority, including two insubordination incidents. Her reprimands were upheld, her ratings remained good, and management and Association leaders criticized the columns. Her causal account and reasonable favorable inferences are credited for sufficiency review; the lower court's contrary evaluation is not an independent fact. Coverage as a labor organization was resolved against the Association. The First Amendment defense was preserved but not decided below.

Old Chief v. United States, No. 95-6556. Argued October 16, 1996; decided January 7, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, which affirmed the federal conviction. The question is whether Rule 403 permitted the Government to identify the name and nature of a prior assault conviction solely to prove felon status when Old Chief offered to admit the complete qualifying status element.

The charges arising from a 1993 confrontation included assault with a dangerous weapon, use of a firearm in a crime of violence and possession of a firearm by a prohibited person under §922(g)(1). The prior judgment described a December 18, 1988 assault causing serious bodily injury and a five-year sentence. Old Chief offered an admission, moved to exclude the name and nature, and renewed his objection when the judgment was introduced. The prosecutor refused the stipulation, and the judge accepted that refusal on the prosecution's general freedom to choose evidence. The jury convicted; the Ninth Circuit upheld the evidentiary ruling without deciding harmlessness. The preserved judgment-record objection is distinct from the requested and later withdrawn credibility instruction. The proposed status instruction required clarification of legal adequacy, but that was not the trial court's ground for refusing the offer.

Walmer v. Department of Defense; Tenth Circuit No. 93-3377. Argued October 16, 1996; decided January 13, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Tenth Circuit, which affirmed denial of a preliminary injunction and dissolved its appellate stay on April 4, 1995, 52 F.3d 851. The questions concern equal protection under the Fifth Amendment, the role of military deference, and the Bill of Attainder Clause in separation under the earlier executive Army Regulation 635-100.

Major Joyce Walmer admitted the past homosexual acts on which the Board of Inquiry proceeded and expressly stipulated that she did not qualify for the regulation's retention exceptions under paragraphs 5-51a(1)–(5) and 5-56. Other initial allegations, including a same-sex marriage, marijuana use and conduct unbecoming, were excluded from the Board proceeding and supply no alternative basis here. The Board recommended honorable discharge; the Board of Review and Secretary adopted that recommendation. The question is preliminary relief against the challenged separation, not a final declaration of policy validity or adjudication under later legislation.

The district court decided likelihood of success without finding irreparable injury, comparative harm or public interest. The court of appeals assumed those other factors only for its modified likelihood inquiry, under which serious, substantial, difficult and doubtful merits questions could warrant deliberate investigation if the remaining factors were satisfied. That assumption was not a finding that they were satisfied. The live preliminary-relief controversy is before the Court on this January 13 calendar; no continuing historical stay, completed discharge or current service-status change is established.

**Castano v. American Tobacco Co.**, Fifth Circuit No. 95-30725, 84 F.3d 734. October Term 1996. Merits decision, January 14, 1997; merits hearing January 14, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, following its May 23, 1996 decision on an accepted interlocutory appeal under 28 U.S.C. §1292(b). The Court reviews the accepted interlocutory appeal, rather than a mandamus proceeding.

The nationwide tobacco-addiction class covers smokers and specified derivative or representative claimants since 1943. The District Court certified core-liability and punitive questions while excluding injury, causation, reliance, defenses and individual compensatory damages. The Court of Appeals reversed and directed dismissal of the class complaint. The class seeks reinstatement; manufacturers seek decertification. The questions concern predominance and superiority; the rigorous analysis required for a novel mass-tort theory; material state-law variations; and management, individual proof and settlement pressure. The separate denial of Rule 23(b)(2) equitable and medical-monitoring certification was not cross-appealed.

**In re Deuel**, Federal Circuit No. 94-1202, 51 F.3d 1552; application Serial No. 07/542,232, Heparin-Binding Growth Factor. October Term 1996. Merits decision, January 14, 1997; merits hearing January 14, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit at the government's request. The petition was held through July 1, 1996; limited review was granted October 7, 1996. No Supreme Court docket number is assigned.

The Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences affirmed the examiner's §103 rejection of claims 4–7 on November 30, 1993. The Federal Circuit reversed on March 28, 1995. Claims 5 and 7 recite particular human placental and bovine uterine cDNA sequences; claims 4 and 6 cover broader DNA genera encoding the identified proteins. The questions concern whether prior protein information and known isolation methods can establish obviousness without prior disclosure of the claimed nucleotide sequence, and when a predictably effective method is sufficient despite uncertainty about precise molecular structure. The actual prior protein disclosure contains only nineteen amino acids, not the complete sequence. The controversy concerns reversal of existing application rejections, not infringement or an order to issue a patent.

On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, whose September 5, 1995 judgment, 67 F.3d 194, affirmed declaratory and injunctive relief against amended §207 of the Indian Land Consolidation Act. William Youpee died on October 19, 1990. His will devised each disputed fractional trust-land interest to one descendant, preserving each existing fraction. Elizabeth G. Curtis v. School Committee of Falmouth. Merits decision, January 21, 1997. Argued November 4, 1996. On writ of certiorari to the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts, which on July 17, 1995, affirmed summary judgment for the school defendants, 420 Mass. 749, 652 N.E.2d 580. The questions concern parental liberty, free exercise, and whether the Constitution requires parental exclusion or notification when this school offers condoms without compelling participation.

The program covers grades seven through twelve. Junior-high students may request free condoms from the nurse and must receive counseling before receipt; the nurse supplies disease-information pamphlets. High-school students may obtain free condoms from the nurse or pay 75 cents at restroom machines; counseling is available on request and pamphlets are available in the nurse's office. The program emphasizes abstinence as the only certain means of avoiding sexually transmitted disease, directs staff to withhold personal opinions, and contains no parental exclusion or notification provision. Program entry is optional and abstention has no grade or disciplinary consequence. Parents and students seek an injunction unless exclusion and notice provisions are added.

counted.event_source:
**Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. v. Federal Communications Commission**, No. 95-992. Merits decision, March 31, 1997. Argued October 7, 1996. On direct appeal from the three-judge District Court for the District of Columbia, 910 F. Supp. 734, after the 1994 remand. The granted question asks whether the developed record establishes advancement and fit under the intermediate scrutiny prescribed for the general full-power must-carry core.

**Statutory setting relevant to fit:** Under 47 U.S.C.§534, systems with 12 or fewer usable activated channels must carry at least three local commercial signals; systems also having 300 or fewer subscribers are exempt from that section only while they delete no broadcast signal. Systems with more than 12 channels carry eligible local commercial signals up to one-third of usable activated capacity. This is not a combined commercial-and-educational ceiling. Substantially duplicative commercial signals already represented in carriage and additional same-network affiliates need not be carried; voluntary duplicates and multiple affiliates count toward the obligation. When eligible stations exceed the required number, the operator selects among them, but cannot substitute low power for full power and must choose the elected network's affiliate with the closest city-of-license reference point to the principal headend.

Section535 adds separate educational duties. Systems with 12 or fewer channels carry one qualified local educational signal and may carry more. Systems with 13–36 carry at least one and need not carry more than three, subject to continued carriage; they may carry more. If no qualified local station is present, the former category must import one qualified educational signal and the latter at least one. For that importation, the smallest systems need not remove programming actually provided on March 29, 1990 but must use the first available channel. All qualified local educational stations carried on that date retain carriage unless operator and station give written waiver consent. Systems above36 channels, including those expanding beyond36, carry requesting qualified local educational stations; a system required to carry three need not add stations substantially duplicating another qualified local educational station requesting carriage. This is not a general three-station cap. A13–36-channel system already carrying a State-network educational affiliate need not add another same-network affiliate whose programming substantially duplicates the carried affiliate.

Commercial distant signals require indemnification of increased copyright liability. A commercial station below the specified headend levels (−45dBm UHF; −49dBm VHF) is excluded if it does not agree to bear the costs of delivering a good-quality or baseband signal. Educational carriage is not required without delivery of a good-quality or baseband signal; its distant-signal indemnity exception concerns adding a signal and expressly does not erase the continued-carriage rule. These are actual programming obligations, including primary video, audio and captions. Commercial carriage includes technically feasible program-related blanking-interval or subcarrier material; educational carriage includes technically feasible program-related ancillary material necessary for disability access, education or language purposes. Other ancillary material remains discretionary. Positioning and availability duties also constrain operation; the law does not merely reserve empty channels. No new dispute over ancillary material, positioning, payment, notice or enforcement is decided.

The reserved low-power duty depends on an insufficient number of full-power local commercial stations: systems with35 or fewer channels carry one qualified low-power station, and larger systems two. Its disputed programming criterion concerns local needs inadequately served because of full-power stations' geographic distance. The separate market-modification factor asks whether another eligible station supplies the community news, sports or events; it is not that requirement imposed on the requesting station. These provisions' independent classifications remain outside the granted question.

counted.event_source:
Camps Newfound/Owatonna, Inc. v. Town of Harrison, No. 94-1988. On review of the Supreme Judicial Court of Maine, 655 A.2d 876, which on April 21, 1995 reversed summary judgment for the camp and sustained the challenged property tax. Argued October 9, 1996; decided May 19, 1997. The question is whether the nonresident-beneficiary condition in Maine's charitable-property exemption discriminates against interstate commerce and whether a subsidy, market-participant or resident-benefit justification sustains it. The Maine nonprofit's 180-acre Christian Science camp recruits nationally; about 95 percent of campers come from outside Maine. Its reported charge is roughly $400 per week and annual property taxes exceed $20,000. It timely pursued state refund and prospective-exemption procedures.

Section 652(1)(A) generally covers real and personal property owned and occupied or used solely for the purposes of benevolent and charitable institutions incorporated by Maine, without loss of exemption merely because of the source of funds or limitations in beneficiary classes, subject to the express nonresident subparagraph. An institution operated principally for nonresidents may exempt no more than $50,000 of current just property value only if the statutory average weekly charge per person does not exceed $30; above that rate it receives no exemption under that subparagraph. The computation divides all tax-year stipends or charges for services, benefits or advantages by all persons receiving them during that year, then divides by the weeks during that tax year when the institution is actually operated principally for nonresidents; §502 defines the tax year. The reported weekly price is not substituted for that statutory computation.

The nonresident subparagraph does not apply to a nonprofit corporation incorporated solely to conduct medical research; that exception does not waive the general exemption's other requirements and is not found applicable to this camp. The paragraph also includes nonprofit nursing, boarding and boarding-care facilities licensed under Title 22, chapter 1665 or its successor; nonprofit community mental-health facilities licensed under Title 34-B, chapter 3; and nonprofit child-care centers incorporated by Maine as benevolent and charitable institutions. Nonprofit means exempt under Internal Revenue Code §501(c)(3). No independent challenge to Maine incorporation, neutral qualification, religious liberty, equal protection or travel rights is decided.

Salazar-Haro v. INS; Third Circuit No. 96-3007, 95 F.3d 309. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1). Submitted and decided June 16, 1997.

Pedro Alejandro Salazar-Haro, a Peruvian citizen who entered in 1978 and obtained permanent-resident status in 1983, was convicted in June 1993 of cocaine-distribution conspiracy and aiding and abetting and received forty-two months' imprisonment. His wife and codefendant was deported in 1994; their three sons were United States citizens. The immigration judge considered rehabilitation, remorse, education, employment, care for the children and cooperation with the Government, but denied discretionary relief in light of sustained and renewed trafficking and the admission that he sold more than ten kilograms of cocaine. The Board of Immigration Appeals rejected the appeal.

The petition for judicial review was filed January 17, 1996, before AEDPA's April 24 enactment. On September 13, 1996, the Third Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. Its observation that it would have denied relief on the merits if it had jurisdiction was hypothetical, not a merits judgment. The final administrative order predates September 30, 1996.

The questions are whether §440(a) withdraws jurisdiction over this pending qualifying deportation petition, whether withdrawal of ordinary review violates due process or constitutional limits on jurisdiction, and what review outside that channel remains available when the Constitution requires it. Those questions are addressed within this record, which identifies no distinct legal defect apart from disagreement with the discretionary balance.

Klehr v. A. O. Smith Corp., No. 96-663. Argued April 21, 1997; decided June 19, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Eighth Circuit, which on June 6, 1996 affirmed summary judgment against the Klehrs, 87 F.3d 231. The questions concern civil RICO's four-year limitations period, the proposed last-predicate-act rule and preserved separate-injury alternatives, and whether fraudulent-concealment tolling dispenses with reasonable diligence. The fact-specific diligence determination and unreviewed state-law dispositions are not reopened.

The Klehrs bought a Harvestore silo in 1974 and allege that its failed oxygen-limiting storage damaged their dairy operation while later representations concealed the source. They filed on August 27, 1993. The lower courts determined that reasonable discovery should have occurred before August 27, 1989. The alleged late representations, continued use, illnesses, lost milk and repairs bear on whether there was a genuinely new injury; their existence alone does not resolve that legal and causal question.

Metropolitan Stevedore Co. v. Rambo, No. 96-272. Argued March 17, 1997; decided June 19, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 81 F.3d 840, decided April 10, 1996, after this Court's earlier review in Rambo I. The questions are whether the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act permits nominal compensation for a significant potential of future injury-related earning-capacity loss despite no current loss, and whether the court of appeals could direct an award without the administrative law judge's necessary finding.

Rambo injured his back and leg in 1980 and received an award based on a stipulated 22.5 percent permanent partial disability. After crane-operator training, he earned about three times his preinjury wages. Metropolitan sought modification on October 30, 1989. The administrative law judge terminated benefits on findings about training, sustained market work, physical demands and earning capacity. The Ninth Circuit directed a nominal award. The stipulated award was not a §8(i) settlement.

O'Dell v. Netherland, No. 96-6867. Argued March 18, 1997; decided June 19, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the Fourth Circuit, which sitting en banc on September 5, 1996 reversed the District Court's Simmons ruling under Teague, 95 F.3d 1214. O'Dell's judgment became final on October 3, 1988, after the Virginia Supreme Court's January 15, 1988 judgment. The granted question is whether Simmons's parole-ineligibility protection is available on habeas review of that final capital judgment.

Virginia argued future dangerousness, and the trial court refused the requested parole-ineligibility instruction and an attempted inquiry whether life meant life without parole. The jury found both future dangerousness and vileness and selected death. It also heard O'Dell describe sixteen years on an earlier parole violation and state that, at his age, he would never get out. The District Court's sentencing relief was expressly conditioned on proof of actual legal parole ineligibility; that predicate was not conclusively established by the order.

United States v. Alaska, No. 84, Original. Argued February 24, 1997; decided June 19, 1997. Original action between the United States and Alaska on exceptions to the Special Master's report, not review of a lower-court judgment. The United States filed in 1979 over Beaufort Sea mineral leasing; Alaska counterclaimed to quiet title within the Petroleum Reserve and Arctic Wildlife Range. Hearings and briefing before the Master followed from 1980 through 1986.

The exceptions concern the coastline used for Alaska's Submerged Lands Act grant, Alaska's claimed ten-mile fringing-island rule in Stefansson Sound, Dinkum Sands' island status, and federal retention of submerged lands within the National Petroleum Reserve and original Arctic Wildlife Range. The Master favored the federal position on the first three issues but Alaska on the Range. The 1957 Range application, the pending-application regulation, statehood and the 1960 final reservation are distinct legal events. No final geographic decree is before the Court for entry today.

Cohen v. Brown University; on writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, No. 95-2205, 101 F.3d 155. Argued May 19, 1997; decided June 23, 1997. Review concerns the three alternative Title IX athletics-accommodation routes, actual unmet interests and the comparative-interest defense, the claimed numerical quota and governmental sex classification, and the scope of equitable relief.

Brown's 1991 restructuring demoted women's gymnastics and volleyball and men's water polo and golf. The District Court entered preliminary protection on December 22, 1992, a merits opinion on March 29, 1995 and final judgment on September 1, 1995. The First Circuit on November 21, 1996 affirmed liability and continuing preliminary protection, vacated the final direction to elevate women's gymnastics, fencing, skiing and water polo to university-funded varsity status, and remanded for another lawful institutional compliance plan. The preliminary two-team relief and later final four-team directive are distinct.

Idaho v. Coeur d’Alene Tribe of Idaho, No. 94-1474. Argued October 16, 1996; decided June 23, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which on December 28, 1994 allowed limited prospective claims against responsible officers while affirming the dismissal of Idaho, its agencies and direct quiet-title relief.

The Tribe alleges federal rights in the beds, banks and waters within the original reservation boundary under an 1873 Executive Order, an 1891 federal statute and an alternative aboriginal-title theory. Its actual prayer seeks exclusive use, occupancy and quiet enjoyment and restraint of state regulatory interference. Review asks whether the Eleventh Amendment bars the prospective officer claims. The lower ruling followed dismissal at the pleading stage and established no ownership. A separate United States action concerns only part of the geography and is not consolidated here.

The Kansas Supreme Court's March 1, 1996 judgment, In re Hendricks, 259 Kan. 246, 912 P.2d 129, invalidated Hendricks's commitment under the 1994 Sexually Violent Predator Act because it considered the statutory mental-abnormality definition constitutionally insufficient. It did not decide the preserved Double Jeopardy or Ex Post Facto claims, presented through Hendricks's cross-petition. The granted questions concern the Act's substantive commitment criteria and whether this confinement is punitive. Both dockets concern the same commitment and judgment.
